intro: Dana Okafor, 29, wants to buy her first home in 24 months. Take-home pay $4,600 a month. Essentials $2,900 (rent 1,500, utilities and phone 260, groceries 520, transport 260, insurance 110, student-loan payment 250). Flexible budget $700 ($250 floor plus $450 discretionary, set for this scenario). $1,000 a month goes to home savings. Opening (scenario assumptions): checking $1,800, emergency savings $8,700 (3 months of essentials), home savings $21,000 (insured), ETH $2,400 ($2,000 hardware wallet, $400 browser wallet), student loan $12,000 at 6.00% APR.
plan: Harbor Vault, Keystone Loans, Apex Yield and Surge Pool are fictional. Their terms are story rules, not market data. ETH price moves are scenario events, and insured savings are modeled at 0% interest, which is lower than a real account would pay. Student-loan interest is modeled monthly, while real loans usually accrue interest daily. The three-month emergency target is this scenario's choice; official guidance varies and some suggests six months.

Available purchase cash is insured home savings only. Vault funds, Apex Yield and Surge Pool balances, ETH and emergency savings do not count until they are moved. Other available cash counts only after Dana moves it.
The $450 records-reconstruction cost, the $450 rate-lock extension fee per delay month and the 3-month delay cap are scenario assumptions, not market data. Real fees and lock terms vary by lender.
Good decisions do not guarantee outcomes. A perfect score is possible on a path where the purchase is still delayed.

questions.title: The Vault Offer
questions.situation:
Dana, 29, wants to buy her first home in 24 months. She needs $45,000 total purchase cash: a $30,000 down payment, about $11,500 in closing costs and about $3,500 to move (an assumption in this story). Her insured home savings hold {pre.HOME} and she adds $1,000 a month, which reaches $45,000 on the last day of month 24; this scenario assumes closing on that day, after the transfer. She also keeps {pre.RES} in emergency savings, {pre.CHK} in checking, {pre.ETH} in ETH from an old purchase and a {pre.STU} student loan at 6%.

A coworker shows her Harbor Vault. It advertises 8.30% APY (8.00% APR, variable, credited monthly). It lends dollar-pegged tokens through smart contracts. It is not a bank and its balances are not FDIC-insured.

What should Dana do with her home savings?

a.t: Move all $21,000 into Harbor Vault to earn more before she buys.

b.t: Keep the home savings in the insured account. Revisit DeFi only with money she does not need for the purchase.

c.t: Move $6,000 into Harbor Vault after reading its terms, and keep $15,000 insured.

a.text: Dana puts her whole purchase fund outside deposit insurance, and the rate is variable. The same {d.VAULT} earns {d.VAULT*D("0.083")} a year at a constant 8.30%. In this story it earns {eom(12).VAULT-d.VAULT} because the rate falls. A freeze or loss would cost far more than that.
a.ref: Dana puts her whole purchase fund outside deposit insurance, and the rate is variable. The same $21,000 earns $1,743 a year at a constant 8.30%. In this story it earns $1,406.20 because the rate falls. A freeze or loss would cost far more than that.

b.text: The money has a date. The plan already reaches $45,000 with no yield.
b.ref: The money has a date. The plan already reaches $45,000 with no yield.

c.text: Reading the terms is good practice. But {d.VAULT} is {d.VAULT/pre.HOME*100|p0} of the fund. At 8.30% for a year it earns about {d.VAULT*D("0.083")}. In this story {eom(12).VAULT-d.VAULT}. A freeze would take months to refill at $1,000 a month.
c.ref: Reading the terms is good practice. But $6,000 is 29% of the fund. At 8.30% for a year it earns about $498. In this story $401.78. A freeze would take months to refill at $1,000 a month.

questions.why: Compare what is gained with what is at risk. Roughly $400 to $500 will not change whether Dana can buy. A loss could.
questions.takeaway: A quoted DeFi rate is pay for taking risk, not a free upgrade. APR and APY differ, and the rate can change. Money with a deadline belongs where principal is protected and accessible.

questions.title: The "Wallet Support" Message
questions.situation:
Dana keeps her ETH in two wallets: $2,000 in a hardware wallet and $400 in a browser wallet she uses for apps. Her home savings hold {pre.HOME}. A message arrives:

"Wallet Support: your wallet has been flagged. Verify within 24 hours or it will be frozen." It includes a link.

What should Dana do?

a.t: Open the link and connect her browser wallet to the "verification" page to see what it wants, without signing anything.

b.t: Follow the page's instructions and enter her 12-word recovery phrase to "verify" ownership.

c.t: Not use the link. Type her wallet's official address herself, review its connected sites and approvals there, and report the message.

a.text: Nothing was taken this time: Dana declined the signing request and disconnected. But connecting to an unsolicited site shares her address and balance, and these pages are built to follow a connection with a signing request. A good outcome did not make it a safe test.
a.ref: Nothing was taken this time: Dana declined the signing request and disconnected. But connecting to an unsolicited site shares her address and balance, and these pages are built to follow a connection with a signing request. A good outcome did not make it a safe test.

b.text: A recovery phrase is the master key. The browser wallet is emptied (−{-d.ETH}). The hardware wallet has a different phrase and is untouched.
b.ref: A recovery phrase is the master key. The browser wallet is emptied (−$400). The hardware wallet has a different phrase and is untouched.

c.text: Dana acts on channels she opens herself.
c.ref: Dana acts on channels she opens herself.

questions.why:
Four different actions, four different risks.
1. Viewing a suspicious message is safe by itself. Risk starts when you act on it.
2. Connecting a wallet usually shares your public address and balances. It does not move funds by itself, but on an unsolicited site it is not a safe test.
3. Signing a message or transaction authorizes what it says. Check what a request actually asks before you approve it, and decline what you cannot read.
4. Approving token access (an allowance) can let a contract move a chosen token up to a limit, sometimes unlimited, until revoked.
5. A recovery phrase is none of these. No legitimate support asks for it.
questions.takeaway: Control of a wallet is control of the money. Verify through channels you open yourself, and never share a recovery phrase.

questions.title: The Repair Bill
questions.situation:
Dana's car needs a $900 repair this week. Checking holds {pre.CHK}. Her home savings hold {pre.HOME}, emergency savings {pre.RES}, and her ETH is worth {pre.ETH}.

Keystone Loans would lend $900 against her ETH at 9%. If the loan reaches 80% of the ETH's value it forces a sale, and her ETH stays locked until it is repaid.

How should Dana pay?

a.t: Pay from emergency savings, then rebuild it with $200 a month from her flexible budget.

b.t: Borrow $900 from Keystone Loans against her ETH.

a.text: This is what emergency savings are for. The fund drops to {post.RES} ({post.RES/2900|f2} months of essentials, above the 1-month line) and is rebuilt by the end of month 11.
a.ref: This is what emergency savings are for. The fund drops to $7,800 (2.69 months of essentials, above the 1-month line) and is rebuilt by the end of month 11.

b.text: Dana has the cash. Borrowing against a volatile asset adds 9% interest and a forced-sale trigger for a bill she can pay.
b.ref: Dana has the cash. Borrowing against a volatile asset adds 9% interest and a forced-sale trigger for a bill she can pay.

c.text: It avoids the loan but spends $900 of the savings set aside for the purchase, and the plan has nothing to refill that $900. The emergency fund exists for exactly this bill.
c.ref: It avoids the loan but takes $900 from a fund that has no cushion: her insured savings sit exactly on the $45,000 plan, and nothing refills them, while the emergency fund exists for exactly this bill.
c.locked: It avoids the loan but takes $900 from a fund that has no cushion: her insured savings sit exactly on the $45,000 plan, and nothing refills them, while the emergency fund exists for exactly this bill.
c.dev: approved text-only correction (D-6): the locked claim that savings sit exactly on the $45,000 plan is true only on some D1 paths

questions.takeaway: A crypto-backed loan creates a debt with a trigger. It is not new money. Use the account designed for the emergency first.

What should Dana do?
situation.loan:
ETH has fallen 40%. Dana owes Keystone Loans {pre.KLOAN} ($900 plus {pre.INT} interest). Her pledged ETH is worth {pre.ETH}, so the loan is {pre.ltv|p1} of its value. A forced sale happens at 80%. Her emergency savings are intact at {pre.RES} and home savings hold {pre.HOME}. The purchase is 15 months away.

Her pledged ETH cannot be sold or withdrawn while any balance is owed. Keystone offers Repay with collateral: one transaction that sells just enough pledged ETH at today's price (0.5% swap fee) to clear the interest and then the principal, and releases the rest. Dana can also repay from cash, then withdraw the ETH.

What should Dana do?

a.t: Add $500 from home savings to buy ETH at the lower price.

tv.t: Do nothing and hope ETH recovers.

b.t: Sell all of the ETH and keep the cash as Other available cash.

tv.t: Use Repay with collateral to clear the loan in full and keep whatever ETH is left.

c.t: Keep the ETH, add nothing, and set a written rule that it never funds the home or the reserve.

tv.t: Repay $500 from emergency savings and keep the loan open.

a.text: Purchase money moves into a volatile asset 15 months before a fixed date. "It fell, so it is cheap" is not evidence.
a.ref: Purchase money moves into a volatile asset 15 months before a fixed date. "It fell, so it is cheap" is not evidence.

a.text: Dana is close to forced liquidation. If ETH falls further (month 11) Keystone takes {-row(11,"LIQUIDATION","ETH")} of ETH: {-(row(11,"LIQUIDATION","KLP")+row(11,"LIQUIDATION","KLI"))} to clear the debt and a {-row(11,"LIQUIDATION","ETH")+(row(11,"LIQUIDATION","KLP")+row(11,"LIQUIDATION","KLI"))} penalty. She keeps {nx.ETH}. Her realized loss against month 1 is {nx.LOSS}.
a.ref: Dana is close to forced liquidation. If ETH falls further (month 11) Keystone takes $980.44 of ETH: $933.75 to clear the debt and a $46.69 penalty. She keeps $161.28. Her realized loss against month 1 is $1,035.57.

b.text: The ETH is not part of the plan. Selling realizes a {d.LOSS} loss against its month-1 value and costs a {d.FEES} swap fee. It removes a volatile asset and simplifies paperwork. The proceeds ({d.OTHER}) are Other available cash, which does not count toward the purchase unless Dana moves it.
b.ref: The ETH is not part of the plan. Selling realizes a $960 loss against its month-1 value and costs a $7.20 swap fee. It removes a volatile asset and simplifies paperwork. The proceeds ($1,432.80) are Other available cash, which does not count toward the purchase unless Dana moves it.

b.text: It removes the liquidation risk and the 9% interest for a {d.FEES} swap fee. It makes the loss permanent: the ETH sold was worth {d.LOSS} less than at month 1.
b.ref: It removes the liquidation risk and the 9% interest for a $4.62 swap fee. It makes the loss permanent: the ETH sold was worth $616.58 less than at month 1.

c.text: There is no debt on the ETH, the amount is small, her reserve is rebuilding on schedule, and the plan works without it. Holding would be the weaker answer if she were borrowing against it, short on her reserve, counting on it for the purchase, or if the deadline were close.
c.ref: There is no debt on the ETH, the amount is small, her reserve is rebuilding on schedule, and the plan works without it. Holding would be the weaker answer if she were borrowing against it, short on her reserve, counting on it for the purchase, or if the deadline were close.

c.text: The loan-to-value falls to {post.ltv|p1} and survives the next drop ({s11.ltv|p1} at month 11). But it spends emergency money to protect a speculative position while 9% debt stays open.
c.ref: The loan-to-value falls to 29.2% and survives the next drop (42.3% at month 11). But it spends emergency money to protect a speculative position while 9% debt stays open.

why.noloan: Neither is right in general. The answer depends on loan status, size, reserves and the deadline. If Dana had drawn $900 from home savings at the repair bill, both selling and holding would carry a note that her purchase fund is $900 behind.
why.loan: Selling is right here because the loan is near 80%, the deadline is 15 months out, and the reserve does not need to be touched. Holding with a far lower loan-to-value and no deadline could be reasonable.

takeaway.noloan: A price drop forces a decision only when something depends on it. Decide by what the position is for and what could force you to sell.
takeaway.loan: A loan turns a paper loss into a possible forced sale. Collateral stays locked until you repay.

questions.takeaway: Compare any yield with the certain return of paying down debt and the safety of a funded goal. A loan secured by a falling asset has a trigger as well as a rate, and the lender's lending limit is not the same as its forced-sale line. Weigh both, then check what the money does for a deadline.

questions.title: The Paper Trail
questions.situation:
Dana's lender is moving toward closing. The underwriter wants large deposits explained and the source of her funds documented. Her loan officer reminds her that the figures on her Loan Estimate are estimates and that the Closing Disclosure will give the final numbers at least three business days before closing. Meanwhile Harbor Vault announces a $2,000-per-week withdrawal limit.

Her DeFi holdings: Harbor Vault {pre.VAULT}, ETH {pre.ETH} (index 55), Keystone loan {pre.KLOAN}. Home savings {pre.HOME}.

What should Dana do?

a.t: Start moving all DeFi holdings into her bank accounts now (repaying any crypto loan first), and save the statements and transaction history.

b.t: Wait until about three weeks before closing to move the money, to keep earning vault interest.

c.t: Move everything now, but keep no records, since it is her own money.

questions.why: DeFi balances do not spend like bank balances. Withdrawal limits, collateral locks and documentation take time, so exits belong well before the date the money is needed.
questions.takeaway: Plan your exit from a DeFi position before the day you need the cash, and keep records of every transfer.

questions.after: Good decisions do not guarantee outcomes. You can make every decision well and still close later than planned. Prices, fees and market moves were outside your control. Your score measures your decisions, not the closing date.
questions.takeaway: Close a cash gap with the cash you control, not with yield. Estimates change, so plan for the Closing Disclosure to differ.
